title: SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email
summary: This RFC specifies an SMTP extension for transporting and delivering email messages that have internationalized email addresses or header information.

eli5.summary: Mail trucks used to carry only English-letter addresses. This teaches them to also deliver mail with addresses in other alphabets.

questions: how to send email to unicode address
how does smtp support unicode email addresses
what happens if a server does not support smtputf8
subtitle: The SMTP extension that lets mail servers agree to carry non-ASCII addresses and UTF-8 headers.

tldr.problem: SMTP envelopes and mailbox names were defined entirely in ASCII, so addresses such as ones with non-ASCII local parts or internationalized domain names could not be sent.
tldr.mechanism: Servers advertise a new EHLO keyword, SMTPUTF8. A client then adds an SMTPUTF8 parameter to MAIL, and UTF-8 may appear in mailbox names, in the headers defined by RFC 6532 and in a few replies.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the experimental approach in RFC 5336 and is a Proposed Standard. A client must not send an internationalized message to a server that does not offer the extension.

today: RFC 6531 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5336, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It works together with RFC 6532, which defines the header format.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6531 defines an extension to the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) so that servers can advertise that they accept and process internationalized email addresses and the internationalized headers of RFC 6532. It is one piece of a larger email internationalization effort. The overview and framework live in RFC 6530, which the text calls the framework document, and a reader is expected to understand it and the base mail specifications first.

The extension does not modify RFC 5321 or RFC 5322. It extends some syntax rules, allows internationalized addresses in the envelope and in trace fields, and requires the existing 8BITMIME extension to be announced and used. It replaces an earlier, experimental approach, RFC 5336, and anyone converting an implementation is told to review the changes in approach carefully.
sections.eli5: Email delivery used to understand only plain English letters. This rule book teaches the delivery system to handle names written with any letters, as long as both sides agree first.

sections.title: The SMTPUTF8 Extension and Negotiation
sections.content:
The service extension is called Internationalized Email and its EHLO keyword is SMTPUTF8. No parameters are defined for the keyword: a server MUST NOT include any, and a client MUST ignore any it sees. A server that lists SMTPUTF8 MUST be fully compliant with the specification, and MUST also support and announce the 8BITMIME extension.

A client that sees the keyword in its EHLO response MAY send mailbox names as UTF-8 strings, and MAY send UTF-8 headers. If the server does not offer the extension, the client MUST NOT transmit an internationalized address or a message with internationalized headers at any level of its MIME structure. Domains in A-label form do not count as internationalized for this rule.

The text then lists what a client may do instead. A Message Submission Agent MAY fix up or transform the message so it conforms to RFC 5321. Otherwise the client SHOULD reject the message, either during the SMTP transaction or by accepting it and then sending a non-delivery notification. A client with extra knowledge MAY requeue the message and try later or try an alternate MX host.
sections.eli5: Before sending a letter with fancy writing, the driver asks the next post office, can you read this? If the answer is no, the driver does not send it there.

sections.title: Parameters on MAIL, VRFY and EXPN
sections.content:
The extension adds one OPTIONAL parameter, SMTPUTF8, to the MAIL command. It takes no value. Its presence says the client is SMTPUTF8-aware and that the envelope has a non-ASCII address, the message is internationalized, or the message otherwise needs SMTPUTF8 support. The maximum length of a MAIL command line grows by 10 characters to make room for it.

If the envelope or message needs the extension, the client MUST supply the parameter. If the client knows neither does, it SHOULD NOT supply it. The reason is practical: the next hop may not support the extension, so using it always risks failure, and early in deployment that risk is high. ASCII-only mail is therefore better sent without it.

The same parameter is added to VRFY and EXPN. There it tells the server that the client can accept UTF-8 in the reply to that one command. Servers that offer the extension may be used with BODY=8BITMIME, or with BODY=BINARYMIME when the server advertises BINARYMIME.
sections.eli5: The sender puts a small sticker on the envelope that says fancy writing inside. Without that sticker, the post office keeps everything plain.

sections.title: Extended Mailbox Syntax and Domain Names
sections.content:
RFC 5321 defined the Mailbox rule using only ASCII. This RFC extends it. The sub-domain rule gains U-label, atext and qtextSMTP gain UTF8-non-ascii, and so does esmtp-value. A UTF-8 string in atext MUST NOT contain any ASCII graphic or control characters. The parsing of the local part and its delimiters is unchanged.

Any domain name looked up in the DNS MUST be processed as specified for Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) in RFC 5890. A client or server MUST either use a Unicode-aware DNS library or convert the name to A-label form, an all-ASCII form with no U-labels, before the lookup.

As a general rule, where RFC 5321 specifies a mailbox this extension requires UTF-8 for the entire string. Where RFC 5321 specifies a domain name, the internationalized name SHOULD be in U-label form if the extension is supported, and otherwise in A-label form.
sections.eli5: Names on envelopes may now use letters from many alphabets. When the computer looks up a town in its address book, it first turns the name into the plain letters the book understands.

sections.title: Reply Codes and UTF-8 in Replies
sections.content:
Rejections follow RFC 5321 codes. If a RCPT command is rejected because it needs an ASCII address, the server returns 553, "mailbox name not allowed". If a MAIL command is, it returns 550, "mailbox unavailable". Servers that support enhanced status codes add X.6.7, non-ASCII addresses not permitted for that sender or recipient. If a message is rejected after the final "." of DATA because a recipient cannot accept internationalized headers, the code is 554 with enhanced code X.6.9. Servers are encouraged to detect this early and fail after RCPT rather than after DATA.

Servers MUST NOT put non-ASCII characters in replies except where the text allows. If a MAIL command carried SMTPUTF8, a server may use UTF-8 in the address of a 251 or 551 reply, and the client MUST accept it. Without the parameter, the server MUST turn such replies into 250 or 550 replies without non-ASCII addresses.

For VRFY and EXPN without the parameter, a server that would need UTF-8 uses 252 or 550, with enhanced code X.6.8. A successful 250 reply MAY include the user name and MUST include the mailbox.
sections.eli5: If the post office has to say no, it uses the usual numbered notes. It only writes in fancy letters when the sender said that is fine.

sections.title: Greeting, Mail Exchangers and Trace Fields
sections.content:
Because a client cannot know whether the server supports SMTPUTF8 until the EHLO response, it MUST send only ASCII domains (LDH labels or A-labels) in the EHLO command. A server giving domain names in its EHLO response MUST also use LDH labels or A-labels.

When a domain has several MX records, the text strongly advises that all or none of the servers support SMTPUTF8. Otherwise unexpected rejections can happen during temporary or permanent failures, which users may see as serious reliability problems.

Trace fields may carry internationalized domain names in U-label form when the extension is used. If a message was or will be sent with SMTPUTF8 on MAIL, a server adding a trace field SHOULD use U-labels. If it was sent without the parameter, trace fields must conform to RFC 5321. The WITH clause uses the new protocol values registered by IANA. The extension is also valid on the submission port and may be used with LMTP.
sections.eli5: Greetings stay in plain letters because nobody knows yet what the other side understands. And if one of a town's post offices cannot read fancy writing, some letters may bounce at odd times.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The security discussion in RFC 6530 applies here. This RFC adds that internationalized addresses will appear in SMTP transaction logs and in trouble ticket systems used by security teams. To avoid loss of data these systems will likely need full UTF-8 support, or an adequate way to map non-ASCII strings to ASCII. Log readers that cannot easily read non-ASCII information SHALL have mechanisms to quickly find the origin or ownership of an internationalized address. VRFY and EXPN are used by some tools to act on suspected spam, so internationalized addresses can affect them too.

IANA added the SMTPUTF8 keyword to the SMTP Service Extension registry, updated the enhanced status codes (adding X.6.7, X.6.8 and X.6.9 and deprecating X.6.10 as a duplicate of X.6.8), and added WITH protocol types such as UTF8SMTP, UTF8SMTPA, UTF8SMTPS, UTF8SMTPSA and the matching UTF8LMTP variants.
sections.eli5: If your mail logs and notebooks cannot read fancy letters, important notes could get lost. So they need to learn the new letters too.
